record.stem: 20260126_Treasuries Look Ready to Break (and what happens when they do)
record.central_claim: The Treasury market looks ready to break to the downside (bond prices falling, yields rising), and when it does, banks will be deregulated to buy unlimited Treasuries with depositor money, leading to severe inflation.

themes.theme: Signals of declining demand for Treasuries

arguments.conclusion: Central banks and funds accumulating gold instead of Treasuries shows trust is shifting to gold.
premises: Gold has been a monetary asset for thousands of years and is still treated as such by central banks.
Treasuries have only been a safe haven temporarily for a few decades.

evidence.item: Gold is on the brink of breaking $5,000 per ounce.

evidence.source_excerpt: official reserves of US debt have now been overtaken by reserves held in gold

arguments.conclusion: Foreign selling of Treasuries, though small in individual amounts, is a signpost of declining demand.
premises: A Danish pension fund announced selling all its Treasury holdings.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent dismissed it as irrelevant in amount.
Gold accumulation by central banks shows a similar trend.

themes.theme: Dollar's real purchasing power decline due to money supply growth

arguments.conclusion: The dollar is weakening in real terms because money supply growth outpaces production.
premises: Money supply is at all-time highs.
Prices of assets and cost of living are rising.
More money chasing the same goods causes inflation.

evidence.item: Money supply keeps making new all-time highs.
evidence.verification_basis: No specific data or timeframe given.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20260126_Treasuries Look Ready to Break (and what happens when they do).txt
evidence.source_excerpt: Money supply keeps on it making new all-time highs.

evidence.item: The dollar is getting much weaker across asset classes and cost of living.
evidence.verification_basis: General assertion without specific metrics or sources.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20260126_Treasuries Look Ready to Break (and what happens when they do).txt
evidence.source_excerpt: whether we're looking at pretty much any asset class, or whether we're looking at the cost of living through things like housing, transportation, or food, the dollar is getting much, much weaker.

themes.theme: Rising Treasury yields and structural debt issues

arguments.conclusion: Long-term Treasury yields are about to break out upwards because lenders demand higher compensation for inflation risk.
premises: Future inflation expectations are high due to government borrowing and money supply growth.
Lenders demand at least the inflation rate to maintain purchasing power.
Short-term yields are suppressed by the Fed, but long-term yields are rising.

evidence.item: The 10-year yield has been getting higher quickly and looks about to break out.
evidence.verification_basis: Chart observation not provided in text.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20260126_Treasuries Look Ready to Break (and what happens when they do).txt
evidence.source_excerpt: the 10-year yield, you can see recently it's been getting higher quickly, and it looks like it's about to break out

analogies.explanation: Illustrates why lenders demand higher interest rates when inflation rises.
analogies.source_speech_filename: 20260126_Treasuries Look Ready to Break (and what happens when they do).txt
analogies.source_excerpt: if I'm going to lend you $100... I'm going to demand at least 5% cuz otherwise, in real terms, I'm losing.

arguments.conclusion: The US government is increasingly reliant on short-term debt because it cannot find enough long-term lenders.
premises: Only 17% of national debt is in bonds (20-30 year).
50% is in notes, 21% in bills.
Almost 72% matures in under 10 years, increasingly at 2 years or less.

evidence.item: Debt composition statistics: 17% bonds, 50% notes, 21% bills, 72% short-term.
evidence.verification_basis: No source cited for debt composition data.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20260126_Treasuries Look Ready to Break (and what happens when they do).txt
evidence.source_excerpt: only 17% of the national debt is currently held in bonds. Bonds are the 30-year treasuries and the 20-year treasuries. And we can see that 50% of the national debt is in notes. Notes are 2-year, 3-year, 5-year, 7-year, and 10-year. And now, 21% of the national debt is in bills. Bills are short-term from 4-week maturity up to 52-week maturity. So, almost 72% of the entire national debt is held at the short end of the curve, maturing in under 10 years.

themes.theme: Federal Reserve and bank deregulation as solution

arguments.conclusion: The Federal Reserve has resumed increasing its balance sheet to buy Treasuries because other buyers are scarce.
premises: Fed started increasing its balance sheet again, as shown in chart.
Previous big round of QE was very unpopular.

evidence.item: Federal Reserve started increasing its balance sheet yet again, as seen at the end of the chart.
evidence.verification_basis: Chart referenced but not provided; no other source given.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20260126_Treasuries Look Ready to Break (and what happens when they do).txt
evidence.source_excerpt: the Federal Reserve started increasing its balance sheet yet again, as you can see at the end of this chart.

arguments.conclusion: The supplementary leverage ratio will likely be permanently removed so banks can buy unlimited Treasuries using depositor funds.
premises: SLR was temporarily suspended in 2020, allowing massive bank buying.
Governor Moran has argued for freeing bank balance sheets.
Banks can earn a spread using depositor money, so they will buy regardless of yield level.

evidence.item: Governor Moran at the Federal Reserve has talked extensively about freeing up banks' balance sheets.
evidence.verification_basis: Reference to source but no excerpt provided.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20260126_Treasuries Look Ready to Break (and what happens when they do).txt
evidence.source_excerpt: Governor Moran at the Federal Reserve has talked about this extensively in speeches and reports that you can find on the Fed's website

evidence.item: SLR was temporarily suspended back in 2020 allowing banks to buy as many treasuries as they wanted.
evidence.source_speech_filename: 20260126_Treasuries Look Ready to Break (and what happens when they do).txt
evidence.source_excerpt: That was temporarily suspended back in 2020 and allowed banks to buy as many treasuries as they wanted, and they did.

themes.theme: Inflation consequences of bank Treasury purchases

arguments.conclusion: If banks buy Treasuries with depositor money, it will cause severe inflation.
premises: Banks will pay depositors very little while earning government yield.
They will drive yields lower, increasing money supply and inflation.
